titulo: Nine seconds at a busy counter
subtitulo: How to actually get seen, how loud is normal, and the permission that undoes years of English-style queueing manners
cena: Six people are pressed against the same counter with no line at all, and the one thing that gets you served is the one thing your instincts are telling you not to do.
decisao: como pedir a vez num balcão sem fila formal — falar no volume certo e fazer contato visual é a ação, não ficar educadamente esperando ser notado
frasePiso: At a busy counter with no line, waiting quietly is not politeness. It's invisibility.

steps.pt: A busy counter often has no formal line — whoever makes eye contact and speaks up gets served next, not whoever waits quietly.
Fourth person deep at a busy stand, no line, everyone talking over everyone. The cook glances up — this half-second matters.
Who's next?
That question is your opening — answer immediately, at a normal speaking volume, not a whisper or a shout.

steps.promptPt: The cook asks who's next. Claim your turn immediately. Speak now.
steps.pt: I'm next, please.
Go ahead.
If two people speak at once and it's unclear who was first, this line settles it without an argument.
I think I got here first.

steps.promptPt: Someone else also claims the turn. Say, calmly, that you think you arrived first. Speak now.
steps.pt: I think I got here first.
The English instinct — 'I was wondering if...' — doesn't read as polite here. It reads as distance, not ready to order.
What can I get you?

steps.promptPt: Order directly, no padding, no apology for existing. Speak now.
steps.es: Deme dos de pastor, por favor.
steps.pinyin: DEH-meh dohs deh pahs-TOR, por fah-BOR
steps.pt: Give me two al pastor, please.
steps.tts: Deme dos de pastor, por favor.

steps.pt: Anything else?

steps.promptPt: The cook asks if that's everything. Close it directly, no padding. Speak now.
steps.pt: No, that's everything.

steps.promptPt: Direct, no padding, at a busy counter. Speak now.
steps.pinyin: meh dah OO-nah OHR-den deh keh-sah-DEE-yahs
steps.pt: Can I have an order of quesadillas?

steps.promptPt: Two words, said fast, while he is already working. Speak now.
steps.pt: Without onion, please.

steps.promptPt: You are not sure if it is the counter or a till. Speak now.
steps.pt: Can I pay here?

steps.promptPt: Smallest possible request, same frame. Speak now.
steps.pt: Can I have a napkin?

steps.es: Yo sigo, por favor. Creo que yo llegué primero. Deme dos de pastor, por favor.
steps.pinyin: yoh SEE-goh, por fah-BOR. KREH-oh keh yoh yeh-GEH pree-MEH-roh. DEH-meh dohs deh pahs-TOR, por fah-BOR
steps.pt: Shadow claiming the turn, defending it, and ordering — all at normal volume, no padding.
steps.tts: Yo sigo, por favor. Creo que yo llegué primero. Deme dos de pastor, por favor.

steps.pt: I02 complete. Yo sigo claims your turn, creo que yo llegué primero defends it, deme plus the item is the whole order.

aprofundar.titulo: Volume and eye contact are the actual queue

secoes.titulo: Dígame and ¿qué le doy? are invitations
secoes.corpo: Both hand you the floor. Recognising them removes the half-second hesitation that costs you your turn at a busy counter.

secoes.titulo: Padding reads as distance, not politeness
secoes.corpo: A direct deme (give me) plus the item, said at a normal volume with eye contact, is the expected register at an informal counter — not curtness.

Banks, government offices and some larger stores do use numbered tickets or a clear line — this counter behaviour is specifically for informal food stalls, market stands and small shops, not everywhere.

permissao: You are allowed to speak first, at normal volume, without an apology attached. Yo sigo and a direct deme are not pushy here — waiting silently and hoping to be noticed is the thing that actually reads as odd.
espelho: Anyone who has ever gotten passed over at a crowded bar back home because they were too polite to catch the bartender's eye already knows exactly what this counter is asking of you — the fix is the same instinct, just deployed here instead of held back.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You've been standing at a busy counter for a few minutes, waiting quietly for someone to notice you're next, and two people who arrived after you get served first.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: They're ignoring me, or my Spanish must be bad enough that they're avoiding me.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: A crowded informal counter often has no visible queue at all — the actual order is whoever speaks up and makes eye contact, not whoever arrived first in silence. Waiting quietly doesn't register as 'next in line' the way it might elsewhere.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Make eye contact with whoever is serving and say yo sigo (I'm next) at a normal, clear volume.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You get served in the actual order of who spoke up, and the interaction resolves in seconds instead of you standing there wondering if you've been forgotten.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not at a bank, government office, or anywhere with a visible numbered ticket or formal line — those places do use strict order, and jumping in verbally there would be the actual mistake.
